_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.point: Bare verbs — no endings, ever
entries.label: Bare verbs
entries.usage: Use the plain dictionary verb for every subject and every time — nothing is ever added to the end of it, and a little word in front (or the time word in the sentence) does the job English endings do.
entries.example: Im ron evri mawnin. — He runs every morning.

entries.point: Progressive a: Mi a ron
entries.label: Happening now (a)
entries.usage: Put a in front of the verb when something is going on right now — Mi a ron, Wa yu a du? — with no 'am' or 'are' anywhere in the sentence.
entries.example: Mi a kuk di dina. — I am cooking the dinner.

entries.point: Past with did: Mi did si im
entries.label: Past (did)
entries.usage: Put did in front of the verb when nothing else in the sentence already shows the thing has happened; with a time word like yeside the plain verb is enough on its own.
entries.example: Mi did si im laas wiik. — I saw him last week.

entries.point: Continuous past: Im did a ron
entries.label: Was doing (did a)
entries.usage: Use did and then a, in that order, for something that was going on at a moment in the past — often when something else interrupted it.
entries.example: Im did a slip wen mi riich. — He was sleeping when I arrived.

entries.point: Completive don: Mi don nyam
entries.label: Finished (don)
entries.usage: Use don when the action is over and done with — Mi don nyam for 'I've already eaten' — either in front of the verb or after the whole verb phrase.
entries.example: Mi don nyam aredi. — I have already eaten.

entries.point: Future: wi and a go: Mi ago kom
entries.label: Future (wi, ago)
entries.usage: Use wi for a plain 'will' and ago (a go) for what you are going to do or what is clearly about to happen — Mi wi kom, It ago rien.
entries.example: Mi wi elp yu tumaro. — I will help you tomorrow.

entries.point: Modals: kyan, hafi, mos, shuda
entries.label: Modals
entries.usage: Use kyan for can and kyaan for can't, hafi for have to, mos for must, and shuda, kuda, wuda for should, could and would.
entries.example: Mi kyan swim gud gud. — I can swim very well.

entries.point: Fi + verb: Mi waan fi go
entries.label: Fi + verb
entries.usage: Put fi in front of a verb for 'to' after words like waan and laan, and also when you mean somebody is supposed to do something — Yu fi lisn to yu mada.
entries.example: Mi waan fi laan Patwa. — I want to learn Patois.

entries.point: The equative copula a: Mi a di tiicha
entries.label: Is a doctor (a)
entries.usage: Use a when you are saying that one thing is another thing — Mi a di tiicha, Im a dakta — and never in front of a describing word.
entries.example: Mi a di nyuu tiicha. — I am the new teacher.

entries.point: The locative copula de: Im de a yaad
entries.label: Is at home (de)
entries.usage: Use de when you are saying where somebody or something is — Im de a yaad, Mi de ya — while a is only for saying what something is.
entries.example: Mi de a yaad tide. — I am at home today.

entries.point: Zero copula with adjectives: Di uman nais
entries.label: Is nice (no a)
entries.usage: Put nothing at all between the thing and the word describing it — Di uman nais, Mi taiyad — because slipping a in there is wrong.
entries.example: Di uman nais. — The woman is nice.

entries.point: Pronouns: mi, yu, im, wi, unu, dem
entries.label: Pronouns
entries.usage: Use these one-shape words wherever they land in the sentence — mi is both 'I' and 'me', im covers he and she alike, and unu is the plural 'you' that English has no word for.
entries.example: Mi a go a skuul. — I am going to school.

entries.point: Plural with dem: di pikni dem
entries.label: Plural (dem)
entries.usage: Put dem after the noun when you mean more than one — di pikni dem — but leave it off when a number or a 'plenty' word already makes it clear, like faiv mango.
entries.example: Di pikni dem de a skuul. — The children are at school.

entries.point: Articles: di, wan, and none
entries.label: Articles
entries.usage: Use di for 'the', and wan for 'a' when it matters that there is just one — but often say no article at all where English needs one, as in Im a tiicha.
entries.example: Di pikni dem a plie. — The children are playing.

entries.point: Possession with fi: a fi mi buk
entries.label: Possession (fi)
entries.usage: Use fi in front of a pronoun to say whose something is — fi mi, fi yu, fi im — while with a person's name you simply set the two words side by side: Jan buk.
entries.example: A fi mi buk dat. — That's my book.

entries.point: Prepositions: ina, pan, outa
entries.label: Prepositions
entries.usage: Use ina for in or inside, pan for on, outa for out of, and plain a for 'to' or 'at' a place — go a maakit, de a yaad.
entries.example: Di pikni dem de ina di yaad. — The children are in the yard.

entries.point: Reduplication: likl-likl, was-was
entries.label: Doubling (gud-gud)
entries.usage: Say the word twice to turn it up or spread it out — swiit-swiit for really sweet, likl-likl for bit by bit, taak-taak for talking on and on.
entries.example: Di mango swiit-swiit. — The mango is really sweet.

entries.point: Negation: no and duon
entries.label: Negation (no)
entries.usage: Put no in front of the verb or its marker to say something is not so — Mi no nuo, Im no de ya — and use duon when telling somebody not to do something.
entries.example: Mi no nuo di ansa. — I don't know the answer.

entries.point: Neva: past negation
entries.label: Didn't (neva)
entries.usage: Use neva rather than no for something that simply did not happen in the past — Mi neva si im means 'I didn't see him', not 'never in my life'.
entries.example: Mi neva tek yu moni. — I didn't take your money.

entries.point: Questions: intonation, we, uu, wa
entries.label: Questions
entries.usage: For a yes/no question keep the ordinary word order and just lift your voice at the end; to ask for detail start with wa, we, uu, wen, ou, umoch or wa mek.
entries.example: Wa yu a du? — What are you doing?

entries.point: Question tags: no chuu? iihn? no?
entries.label: Question tags
entries.usage: Tack no chuu?, iihn? or no? onto the end of a statement when you want the other person to agree with you.
entries.example: Di mango dem swiit, no chuu? — The mangoes are sweet, aren't they?

entries.point: Se after talk and know: Im tel mi se…
entries.label: Saying that (se)
entries.usage: Use se to hook on what somebody said, knows, thinks or heard — Im tel mi se yu gaan — exactly where English would say 'that'.
entries.example: Im tel mi se yu naa kom. — He told me that you're not coming.

entries.point: Serial verbs: ron go bring it kom
entries.label: Serial verbs
entries.usage: String the verbs straight together with no 'and' or 'to' between them — Ron go kaal im, Tek it kom ya — with go and kom on the end to show which way it moves.
entries.example: Ron go kaal yu faada. — Run and call your father.

entries.point: Predicate cleft: A tiif im tiif it
entries.label: Stressing the verb
entries.usage: When somebody doubts that the thing really happened, say a plus the verb first and then the whole sentence again — A tiif im tiif it insists that stealing is exactly what he did.
entries.example: A tiif im tiif di moni. — He STOLE the money (stealing is what he did).

entries.point: Focus fronting: A we yu a go?
entries.label: Fronting for focus
entries.usage: Move whatever you want to spotlight to the front and put a before it — A yu mi a taak to for 'it's YOU', A we yu a go? for 'where exactly'.
entries.example: A yu mi a taak to, no im. — It's YOU I'm talking to, not him.

entries.point: Mek: let, make, and let's
entries.label: Let, let's (mek)
entries.usage: Use mek for let, make and let's — Mek wi go, Mek mi si, Yu a mek mi liet — with a pronoun and then a plain verb behind it.
entries.example: Mek wi go a di bich! — Let's go to the beach!

entries.point: Conditionals: ef … wuda
entries.label: If (ef, wuda)
entries.usage: Use ef and then an ordinary sentence for a real 'if' — Ef it rien, wi stie a yaad — and ef with did plus wuda for something that never actually happened: Ef mi did nuo, mi wuda kom.
entries.example: Ef it rien, wi naa go. — If it rains, we're not going.

entries.point: Existentials and weather: it av, wan … de
entries.label: There is (it av)
entries.usage: Say there is something with it av, or by putting de after the thing — Nof mango de pan di tri — and describe weather with no 'it' at all: Rien a faal.
entries.example: It av wan gud shap a toun. — There's a good shop in town.

entries.point: The continuum: Patwa to Jamaican English
entries.label: Deep vs standard
entries.usage: Pick how deep to go for the situation — Im en a nyam at the deep end, Im did a eat in the middle, He was eating at the English end — and listen for the giveaways: en or did, nyam or eat, unu or you all.
entries.example: Deep Patwa fi 'he was eating': Im en a nyam. — Deep Patois for 'he was eating': Im en a nyam.

entries.point: Proverbs: Wanti wanti kyaan getti
entries.label: Proverbs
entries.usage: Drop a whole proverb into a conversation the way a Jamaican speaker does — learn each one word for word, with its rhythm, because it stands in for a whole argument.
entries.example: Wan wan koko ful baskit. — One by one (cocoyam by cocoyam) fills the basket.

entries.point: Iyaric: I-an-I and Rasta wordcraft
entries.label: Iyaric (Rasta)
entries.usage: Reach for the Rastafari words when the talk is conscious or reasoning — I-an-I in place of mi and wi, overstand for understand, downpressor for oppressor, Ital for pure food.
entries.example: Rasta seh: I-an-I a go a di hills. — Rasta says: I (we) am going to the hills.

entries.point: Written Patwa: Cassidy spelling and dialect literature
entries.label: Spelling (Cassidy)
entries.usage: Write the one-sound-one-letter Cassidy way used in this course — di, likl, kyaan, uman — but expect likkle, cyaan and ooman when people type Patois online.
entries.example: Cassidy spelling fi 'little': likl. — Cassidy spelling for 'little': likl.
